passage: Wasim leaned into the microphone. "Honestly, Devika, my first two years of college looked like a mess from outside. I started in commerce, switched to psychology, sat in on sociology. I joined the mountaineering club, the debate society and a street-theatre group, all in one semester. My uncle kept asking when I'd settle. What made it different from just drifting was a notebook. After every change I wrote three things: what I liked, what drained me, what I valued. My friend Harpreet hopped around just as much but never paused to ask why, and at twenty-two Harpreet is still waiting for something to click. For me, after a summer volunteering at a village school, the notebook kept saying the same thing: teaching, people, fairness. So this year I finally chose education studies. I didn't pick it off a list. I tested my way to it."

qa.a: What Wasim liked, what drained Wasim, and what Wasim valued.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Wasim's exploring?
qa.a: The summer volunteering at a village school, after which the notebook kept pointing to teaching, people and fairness, so Wasim chose education studies.

qa.q: How might Wasim's uncle see those first two years?

passage: My name's Jagdish, and I've shared a flat with Afreen for two years, so I've seen her go through a lot of versions. In first year she was pre-law. Then she took a gap semester to work on a turtle project on the coast. Back at college she switched to environmental science, joined the photography club and quit it, and turned down an internship her father had arranged. From outside it could look like she can't decide anything. But she doesn't just drift. On Sunday nights she sits on the balcony with a list and crosses things out. Last week she told me, "I've ruled out law and pure lab work. I like the field, and I like explaining it to people." I can't know what's going on in her head. But the list keeps getting shorter.

qa.q: Where did Afreen go during her gap semester?
qa.a: To work on a turtle project on the coast.

qa.q: How does Afreen seem to feel about her direction now?
qa.a: She seems more confident and hopeful, telling Jagdish she has ruled out law and pure lab work and likes the field and explaining it.

qa.q: What habit keeps Afreen's exploring from becoming pure drifting?
qa.a: Sitting with a list on Sunday nights and crossing things out, so each experience helps narrow her choice.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: September. Vikas quit engineering after one term, joined the film club, then a cycling group, and signed up for Spanish. When Deepak asked what the plan was, Vikas laughed. "No plan. I'm exploring." By December he had dropped all three and spent most days in bed scrolling videos. Mid-January. Deepak found him in the canteen staring at a blank form for next semester. "I'm stuck," Vikas admitted. "I've tried loads, but I never asked myself what any of it meant." March. Vikas kept a notebook now. Each week he tried one thing on purpose and wrote down what stayed with him. The film club kept coming back: not the watching, the editing. He enrolled in a media course, and for once it felt like his own choice.

qa.a: He spent most days in bed scrolling videos.

qa.a: He tried one thing on purpose each week and wrote down what stayed with him, which led him to editing and a media course.

qa.a: In September Deepak heard 'no plan', but by March Deepak sees Vikas making a considered choice, so Deepak is likely relieved and hopeful.

grounding: A college student's exploring first stalls into drifting, then becomes reflective, leading him to a chosen direction.

passage:
"Ojas, your mother says you've switched from physics to history and she's worried. Let your Harish Mama tell you something.
At nineteen I did commerce for a year, hated it, and moved to botany. I spent one summer with a travelling theatre group in Karnataka and another at a teacher-training camp in the hills. My father called me a butterfly.
But every evening I wrote in a notebook. What did I enjoy today? What made me lose track of time? By third year one answer kept coming back: explaining things to children. So I became a teacher, and I chose it; nobody handed it to me.
My roommate Dilip also tried everything, but he never asked himself anything. He's still trying things, at sixty.
So switch if you must. Just keep a notebook."

qa.q: What did Harish's father call him?
qa.a: His father called him a butterfly.

qa.q: Why does Harish Mama bring up his roommate Dilip?
qa.a: He wants Ojas to see that exploring without reflection can stall, because he worries Ojas might drift instead of choose.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Harish's college years?
qa.a: Noticing in his notebook that explaining things to children kept coming back, which let him choose teaching for himself.

qa.q: How might Ojas's mother feel after hearing this story?
qa.a: She might worry less about the switch to history, as long as Ojas is reflecting and not just drifting.

grounding: An uncle recalls exploring subjects and summers in college with nightly reflection that led to a chosen career, unlike a roommate who drifted.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
The portal for choosing a major crashed at two, and the deadline was five. Nikita, twenty, grabbed an umbrella and ran across the flooded quad to the registrar's office, a paper form in a plastic sleeve.
In the queue she found her senior, Tanuja. "Still undecided? You've done economics, a term of design, and that rural health survey."
"I know. Everyone says I'm wasting time." Nikita looked at the form. "But on the survey I kept redrawing the charts at midnight because the villagers couldn't read them. Nobody asked me to. It's the only thing I've never got bored of."
"So?"
"So information design. Economics as a minor, for the numbers." She wrote it, rain dripping onto the edge of the paper.
Tanuja grinned. "That took you two years."
"It took two years to know it."

qa.q: When did the portal crash, and when was the deadline?
qa.a: The portal crashed at two, and the deadline was five.

qa.q: What does Nikita's memory of redrawing charts at midnight show about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she had been reflecting on what truly held her interest, not just drifting between subjects.

qa.q: What made Nikita's exploring lead somewhere instead of stalling?
qa.a: She noticed what she never got bored of and used it to choose, turning two years of trying things into a clear decision.

qa.q: How might the people who said Nikita was wasting time see her choice now?
qa.a: They might see that the years of switching gave her a real reason for her major, not just a delay.

grounding: A college student who tried several subjects reflects on what held her interest and commits to a major before a rainy deadline.
